planting.note: Transplant container-grown rosettes in spring into lean, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; give plants room to reach full size before the trunk and spines develop.

directions: This Arizona mountain native forms a solitary rosette of stiff gray-green leaves armed with reddish-brown marginal teeth and a stout terminal spine, rarely producing offsets until flowering age. Give it full sun and lean, rocky, sharply drained soil, since it comes from elevations with distinct wet and dry seasons and resents being kept constantly moist. After many years of slow growth it sends up a tall branched flower stalk lined with golden-yellow blossoms, then the rosette dies, leaving any basal pups to continue the clump. It tolerates brief winter cold into the high teens Fahrenheit once established in a well-drained site.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown offsets in spring into fast-draining soil in full sun; this coastal species spreads by rhizomatous pups to form colonies and tolerates salt spray and wind but not hard freezes.

directions: Native to coastal bluffs and scrub from San Diego County into Baja California, this agave forms broad rosettes of dark green to olive leaves patterned with the imprint of neighboring leaves and tipped in a heavy reddish-brown spine. It spreads readily by rhizomatous offsets to form dense colonies, making it useful as a spiny barrier planting or erosion-control mass on dry coastal slopes. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage; it tolerates salt spray and wind but is more sensitive to hard freezes than inland desert agaves, so reserve it for mild winter climates. Flower stalks carry maroon-tinted blooms on a tall branched panicle before the flowering rosette declines.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown rosettes in spring into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; protect from prolonged winter wet and hard freezes.

directions: Native to limestone cliffs in Oaxaca, Mexico, Ghost Agave produces broad, undulating, pale gray-green leaves with small, widely spaced marginal teeth and a relatively soft terminal spine compared to more heavily armed agaves. In habitat it often grows sideways or pendant from rock faces, but in cultivation it forms a tidy, symmetrical rosette well suited to raised beds, rock gardens, and containers. Plant in full sun in lean, fast-draining soil and water sparingly, since prolonged wet soil quickly leads to rot. It is less cold-hardy than many desert species, so protect it from hard freezes and prolonged winter rain.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Transplant container-grown rosettes or offsets in spring into sharply drained, mineral soil in full sun; allow space for the open rosette and loose colonies it forms over time.

directions: Found on limestone hillsides in eastern Mexico, this agave forms broad, glossy, yellow-green leaves lined with widely spaced, often paired, chestnut-brown teeth large enough to resemble small wooden spikes, giving rise to its common name. It spreads at the base to form loose colonies over time rather than remaining strictly solitary, and its bold, open rosette makes a dramatic accent in a xeriscape border. Grow in full sun in sharply drained, mineral soil and keep irrigation minimal, since it is adapted to seasonal drought. Established plants handle brief cold snaps into the low 20s Fahrenheit without serious damage.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown offsets in spring into gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; its compact mature size suits pots, raised beds, and small courtyard plantings.

directions: Native to rocky slopes in Oaxaca and Puebla, Mexico, this compact agave forms a dense, symmetrical rosette of broad, glaucous blue-gray leaves tipped with a dark reddish-brown terminal spine and lined with smaller teeth along the margins. Its manageable size makes it one of the most widely grown small to medium agaves for pots, raised beds, and tight garden spaces, and it is the wild parent of several popular variegated nursery selections such as 'Kichijokan'. Plant in full sun in gritty, fast-draining soil and water only when the root zone has dried out completely. It is monocarpic, eventually sending up a tall flower spike after many years before the rosette dies, typically leaving offsets behind.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown divisions or pups in spring into average to sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Native to dry woodlands and sandy clearings from Virginia south into Georgia, Weakleaf Yucca forms a low, stemless rosette of narrow, blue-green leaves that bend or droop toward their tips rather than standing rigidly upright like many of its relatives. This softer habit, combined with leaf margins that shed fine curling threads rather than carrying a dangerous point, makes it a comparatively safe choice near paths and patios. In early summer it sends up a tall, branched stalk of nodding, creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers well above the foliage. Plant in full sun in average to sandy, well-drained soil; it is extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, and slowly produces offsets that can be divided to start new plants, as seen in the golden-margined selection 'Garland's Gold'.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring into deep, well-drained soil in full sun; allow room for the eventual trunk and wide rosette spread.

directions: Widespread across the high plains and hillsides of central and northern Mexico, this tree-forming yucca eventually develops a thick, often branched trunk topped with dense rosettes of stiff, fibrous-margined, blue-green leaves. It is among the largest and fastest-growing of the tree yuccas, commonly planted as a bold architectural specimen or street tree in warm, dry climates. Give it full sun and deep, well-drained soil with room to develop its eventual trunk and spread, since crowded or soggy sites slow growth and invite rot. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant but are best reserved for essentially frost-free to lightly frosted areas, since hard freezes can damage the growing tips.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown rosettes in spring into rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; position away from foot traffic since the leaf tips are sharply pointed.

directions: Native to limestone slopes of the Chihuahuan Desert in West Texas and northern Mexico, this yucca develops a stout, often solitary trunk crowned with a dense rosette of narrow, rigid, blue-green leaves tipped in a sharp point. Established plants produce one of the showiest flower displays in the genus, a massive, densely packed panicle of creamy-white blossoms held well above the foliage in late spring. Plant in full sun in rocky, sharply drained soil and avoid any supplemental irrigation beyond occasional deep watering during extended drought, since wet conditions promote crown and root rot. It is reliably cold-hardy into the single digits Fahrenheit once established, tolerating far colder winters than tropical tree yuccas.
